planting.note: Grow on a moss pole or totem to encourage the largest, most heavily fenestrated adult leaves; without support it sprawls and bushes out horizontally instead of climbing.

directions: This trade form of the swiss cheese vine carries broader, rounder leaves than the standard narrow-leaved plant, with a width-to-length ratio closer to one-to-two rather than the elongated, lance-like blade of the common form. Its holes are proportionally larger and more numerous per leaf, and the thicker stems support a bushier, more horizontally sprawling habit rather than the tall, wiry climb typical of the species. Give it a moss pole if an upright, more fenestrated specimen is wanted, since without support it tends to mound and trail rather than ascend. The glossy, smooth-textured leaf surface distinguishes it from the more crinkled, narrower-leaved forms commonly sold under the same species name.

planting.note: Give it a tall moss pole or trunk-like totem; this species needs real climbing height before it fenestrates, and mature stems arrange their leaves in a distinctive overlapping fan.

directions: Native from Panama south through the Andes to Bolivia, this vigorous climber holds a narrower, smoother-textured, more lance-shaped leaf than Monstera deliciosa, with a subtle glossy sheen and a clean, uniform green free of silver or cream patterning. Juvenile plants produce small, entire (unholed) leaves and show no fenestration at all until the stem begins climbing in earnest, at which point the foliage enlarges substantially and develops neat, oval perforations arranged in tidy rows along either side of the midrib. Mature stems tend to hold their large leaves in an overlapping, fan-like arrangement at the growing tip, a habit that sets flowering-size specimens apart from most other climbing Monstera species in cultivation. It is a fast grower once established on a support and tolerates slightly cooler night temperatures than many of its more tender relatives.

planting.note: Start young plants pressed flat against a rough totem or bark slab to encourage the shingling juvenile habit, then transition to a tall moss pole so the mature, one-sided pinnate leaves can develop.

directions: Ranging from Costa Rica to Bolivia, this species passes through one of the most dramatic transformations in the genus: as a juvenile it presses small, overlapping, oval leaves flat against a host trunk in the classic shingling habit shared with a handful of other Monstera species, giving no hint of what follows. Once the stem climbs clear of that stage, the leaves lengthen dramatically and become pinnately cut, but unusually the division into lobes typically develops along only one side of the leaf while the other side stays comparatively whole, producing an asymmetric, feathered silhouette unlike the evenly fenestrated leaves of Monstera deliciosa or Monstera adansonii. Adult foliage can extend to several feet in length on a well-climbed specimen. Because the shingling phase depends entirely on tight contact with a flat, rough surface, young plants grown loose in a pot without that contact will skip straight to a lax, non-shingling juvenile form.
sources: Exotic Rainforest species profile: Monstera spruceana

planting.note: Let stems hang and cascade rather than forcing them upright; in habitat this diminutive species dangles from branches, so a hanging basket or an angled totem it can drape over suits it better than a straight moss pole.

directions: Found from southern Costa Rica into Colombia, this is one of the smallest-growing and least fenestrated species commonly grown in the genus: its dull green, leathery leaves stay entire (never developing holes or splits) and are strongly asymmetric, lance-shaped, and two to five times longer than they are wide, with a slightly curved, sickle-like profile. Rather than climbing straight up a host trunk, mature stems characteristically hang and dangle from tree branches, holding their fruit upright even as the foliage drapes downward, a growth habit distinct from the strongly ascending posture of Monstera deliciosa or Monstera standleyana. Juvenile plants pass through a shingling stage low on the host before elongating into these pendent, hanging shoots. Its small stature and lack of fenestration make it a good fit for growers with limited overhead space who still want an authentic species Monstera.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) - Monstera pittieri

planting.note: Press young cuttings against a rough, flat bark slab or cork totem so the stem can shingle tightly against it; the corky raised bumps on the leaf undersides develop best on plants grown in bright shade with high humidity.

directions: Native from Mexico and Belize south to Panama, this species is named for the raised, corky tubercles that stud the undersides of its leaves near the primary veins, giving the foliage a distinctive sandpaper-like texture unlike the smooth leaf surfaces of most other Monstera in cultivation. Young plants shingle tightly against a host trunk with deeply cordate, irregularly angled, fenestrated leaves 8 to 14 inches long, then shift at maturity to shorter-stemmed, oval leaves that lose the holes entirely and stay simple and entire. Unusually for an aroid, its fruit hangs downward like a pendant rather than standing erect. The dramatic shift from heavily fenestrated juvenile foliage to plain, unholed adult leaves makes this one of the more identification-challenging species for collectors who only know it from cuttings sold in the juvenile shingling stage.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) - Monstera tuberculata
